questiontext.text: In the triple (COO) representation of a sparse matrix, what does each stored record contain?

answer.text: (row, col, value) for each nonzero entry

feedback.text: Correct — each nonzero is a (row, column, value) triple.

answer.text: (row, col) for every entry, including zeros

feedback.text: Zeros are not stored, and the value is needed too.

answer.text: Only the value of each nonzero entry

feedback.text: Without row and column you cannot locate the entry.
That is exactly what the sparse form avoids.

generalfeedback.text: The coordinate (triple) form keeps one (row, col, value) record per nonzero and discards all zeros.

questiontext.text: Sparse (triple) storage saves the most space when...

answer.text: most of the matrix entries are zero

feedback.text: Correct — few nonzeros means few triples to store.

answer.text: the matrix is completely full of nonzeros

feedback.text: Then triples cost more than a dense array.
Shape does not decide sparsity.

answer.text: all entries are equal to one

feedback.text: That is a dense matrix, not a sparse one.

generalfeedback.text: The win comes from storing only nonzeros; a nearly full matrix wastes space in triple form.

questiontext.text: What does transposing a sparse matrix do to each stored triple?

answer.text: swaps its row and column indices

feedback.text: Correct — entry (r, c, v) becomes (c, r, v).
Transpose does not change values.
Nonzeros stay nonzero after transpose.
Values are unchanged.

generalfeedback.text: Transpose reflects across the diagonal: (r, c, v) becomes (c, r, v), values untouched.

questiontext.text: What is the time complexity of fast transpose on a sparse matrix with t nonzeros and c columns?

feedback.text: Correct — count entries per column, then place each once.
That is the naive scan-per-column transpose, not the fast one.
That is dense transpose cost, ignoring sparsity.
Every nonzero must be touched at least once.

generalfeedback.text: Fast transpose first counts nonzeros per column, computes starting positions, then relocates each triple once: O(c + t).

questiontext.text: The triple representation stores only the nonzero entries of the matrix.

feedback.text: Correct — zeros are implied and never stored.
Only nonzeros are kept; zeros are omitted.

questiontext.text: Fast transpose is slower than repeatedly scanning the whole triple list once per column.

feedback.text: Fast transpose is faster: it counts per column instead of rescanning.
Correct — fast transpose O(c + t) beats the naive O(c * t) scan.

questiontext.text: The operation that swaps the row and column index of every entry, turning (r, c, v) into (c, r, v), is called the matrix ______.

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.
Accepted — the triple form is where this swap is applied.

questiontext.text: Which statements about the triple (COO) sparse representation are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: It saves space when the matrix is mostly zeros

feedback.text: Yes — fewer nonzeros mean fewer triples.

answer.text: Fast transpose runs in O(columns + nonzeros)

feedback.text: Yes — by counting entries per column first.

answer.text: It must store an entry for every cell, including zeros

feedback.text: No — zeros are never stored.
No — transpose only swaps row and column indices.

generalfeedback.text: Triples store only nonzeros, transpose swaps indices (not values), and fast transpose is O(c + t).
